🤔TIMELINES, PATTERNS & THE DEBRIEF

I'm not a lawyer. I'm not an intelligence officer. I'm not a government official. I'm a guy who works in construction who has spent six years reading primary sources, tracking enforcement actions, and building a workbook that now contains more than six hundred and thirty documented events across five countries and more than forty jurisdictions.

I'm not going to ask you to believe me. I'm going to ask you to look at what the government itself has said, in its own documents, on its own letterhead, and decide for yourself whether what you're watching on the news makes more sense once you've seen the blueprint underneath it.

And at the end, I'm going to show you the evidence that cuts against me. Because if I only show you the parts that fit, I'm not an analyst. I'm a salesman.

Here is the case. 

EXHIBIT A  They built the machine.

After September 11, 2001, the United States government constructed a financial surveillance and enforcement architecture unlike anything in human history. This is not disputed. The agencies exist. The laws were passed. The executive orders are published.

They created the legal authority to trace every dollar moving through the global banking system. Section 314 of the PATRIOT Act gave them the ability to query every financial institution in America about any person, simultaneously.

They created the ability to map networks. Treasury's Office of Intelligence and Analysis established December 2003 describes its own analysts as using all-source intelligence to, and I'm quoting their own press releases, "map illicit financial networks."

They created the ability to cut anyone off. Section 311 gives them the power to designate any foreign financial institution as a money laundering concern and sever its access to the U.S. dollar. They tested it on small banks in Myanmar in 2003. They tested it on Banco Delta Asia in 2005. By 2007, the weapon was battle-tested.

They created the ability to freeze assets without warning. The PATRIOT Act amendment to IEEPA allows blocking pending investigation. Freeze first, notify later. Every OFAC action since 2001 traces to this authority.

And they connected all of it together. In September 2004, FinCEN signed a formal memorandum of understanding with every major federal banking regulator the Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC, OTS, NCUA. The MOU established a standing, bidirectional information pipeline. Law enforcement intelligence could flow to banking supervisors. Examination data could flow back. The MOU specifically contemplated financial crime issues with and these are the document's exact words "national systemic impact on the banking industry."

By 2006, FinCEN was connected to the SEC. By 2007, OFAC compliance was embedded inside Federal Reserve safety-and-soundness examinations. By July 2008, the Fed and SEC signed a direct information-sharing agreement covering mortgage markets, credit derivatives, securitization, and counterparty relationships.

Eighteen agencies. Created or reorganized between 2001 and 2008. Covering terrorism, finance, borders, intelligence, military command, WMD, cyber, and cargo. All built around the same operational concept: find the network, map the network, track the network, isolate the network, dismantle the network. 

I didn't write those documents. They did. And they published them.

The machine exists. That is not a theory.

EXHIBIT B The authorities that matter never get turned off.

Let me be precise here, because precision is the whole point.

Emergency authorities under IEEPA do get terminated. Zimbabwe's was ended in March 2024. Côte d'Ivoire's in September 2016. Liberia's in November 2015. Of seventy-seven national emergencies declared under IEEPA since 1977, forty-six are still running as of last year. Thirty-one were shut down.

So the authorities are not permanent. Somebody decides.

Now look at which ones nobody ever decides to end.

Narcotics trafficking  declared 1995. Still active. Terrorism  declared 2001. Still active. Transnational criminal organizations  declared 2011. Still active. Malicious cyber activity declared 2015. Still active. Serious human rights abuse and corruption declared December 20, 2017. Renewed every single year since, by two administrations that agreed on nothing else. Election interference declared 2018. Still active. Cartels  renewed July 16, 2026, eight weeks ago.

Zimbabwe gets released. The network authorities never do.

That's not a coincidence of paperwork. That's a choice, made annually, in writing, published in the Federal Register, by presidents of both parties who were actively trying to erase each other's legacies on everything else.

The government currently holds simultaneous emergency authority over every category of threat this workbook tracks. All at once. Right now.

And the machine that uses those authorities FinCEN, OFAC, the entire post-9/11 financial warfare stack has been running continuously for twenty-five years.

EXHIBIT C  They let the network operate.

This is the part people struggle with. Why didn't they stop it sooner?

Because that's not how intelligence operations work. And we know this because the government has publicly admitted to doing exactly this repeatedly.

ANOM. The FBI secretly built and ran an encrypted phone platform. They let criminals adopt it. For three years, drug traffickers, arms dealers, and money launderers used it thinking it was secure, while every message went straight to law enforcement. When they rolled it up: eight hundred arrests. Sixteen countries. One morning.

Hansa Market. Dutch police secretly seized a darknet marketplace. They didn't announce it. They ran it for a month. When AlphaBay was publicly taken down, users flooded to Hansa straight into the trap. Thousands of identities harvested.

EncroChat. French and Dutch intelligence penetrated the encrypted phone network used by organized crime across Europe. Monitored it for months. Then rolled it up. Six thousand five hundred arrests.

The crypto enforcement record we track shows an average of eight point seven years between the crime and the prosecution. Not because prosecutors are slow. Because they were watching. Building the map. Letting the blockchain record every transaction. And then prosecuting when the map was complete.

This is the "let it ride" doctrine. You find the network. You don't kick down the door. You let it operate. Every transaction is a receipt. Every connection reveals another name. Every day the network runs is another day of evidence building itself.

The criminals do the work for you. They think nobody is watching. So they get comfortable. They get sloppy. They bring in their cousins, their bankers, their lawyers. And every single connection goes into the map.

EXHIBIT D Then they activated. Everywhere.

In December 2017, Executive Order 13818 pointed the machine at a new target. Not just terrorists. Not just rogue states. The transnational criminal network class operating through legitimate institutions. Across borders. Across continents. Everywhere the network touches.

What we have documented is not five countries acting alone.

It is five sovereign powers the United States, China, Russia, Saudi Arabia, and India who are geopolitical adversaries on nearly every other issue, conducting parallel enforcement operations against the same network class, on overlapping timelines, without opposing each other's enforcement actions. That is the spine.

But the spine is connected to a body.

Forty-plus jurisdictions are participating in the same enforcement wave. Not because one country told them to. Because the network class operates in all of them, and the enforcement architecture reaches all of them.

INTERPOL's Operation First Light, this year five thousand eight hundred and eleven arrests, two hundred and ninety-three million dollars intercepted, ninety-seven nations, in one operation running January through April.

And here is the detail nobody reports. INTERPOL has run First Light since 2014. It is funded by China's Ministry of Public Security. With support from ASEANAPOL, the Gulf Cooperation Council police organization, and Europol.

Read that again. A Chinese-funded, INTERPOL-coordinated operation producing arrests in ninety-seven countries including the United States. Beijing pays for it. Brussels supports it. Riyadh participates. Washington participates.

You are told these countries are on the brink of war with each other. They are co-funding the same police operation.

The extended cooperation arc documented in our workbook three hundred and forty agencies, sixty-five countries, four point four billion dollars in lifetime frozen assets.

And here's the cleanest single sequence in the entire workbook. One organization Cartel Jalisco Nueva Generación. Eleven separate enforcement actions. Nine different sovereign governments. Seven agencies. Six distinct legal instruments. Eighteen months. Nobody announced a joint task force. Nine sovereigns hit the same organization anyway.

The European Union and United Kingdom issuing joint sanctions against thirty-three Russian FSB cyber targets in a single coordinated action. The United States and United Kingdom publishing joint enforcement guidance for the first time. The United States and Saudi Arabia jointly sanctioning Hezbollah financial networks. Canada and the United States dismantling Punjab-based transnational crime syndicates together. Australia sentencing Sam Gor network leaders to fifteen years.

Twenty-plus bilateral deals signed since April 2025 not trade deals. Enrollment deals. Each one contains enforcement cooperation provisions, anti-money-laundering requirements, intelligence-sharing architecture. Jordan. Vietnam. South Korea. Japan. The UAE. Each country that signs isn't just making a trade agreement. It's joining the enforcement infrastructure.

This is not five countries having a coincidence.

The phrase I use is coordinated capacity, not central command. Nobody is running a war room telling forty countries what to do on Tuesday. What is happening is that forty-plus countries independently possess the same enforcement tools, face the same network class embedded in their own institutions, and are activating against that network on timelines that converge because the network itself is global, and the cleanup has to be global to work.

You cannot clean a house by sweeping one room if the dirt tracks through every hallway. You sweep every room. At the same time. Or the dirt just moves.

In the last eighteen months alone:

Six Latin American criminal organizations designated as Foreign Terrorist Organizations with the first financial network sanctions hitting within thirty-five days of designation. A Mexican cartel co-founder sentenced to life with a fifteen billion dollar forfeiture the largest in American history. A trade statute from 1930 used for the first time in ninety-six years with the required commission re-stacked three days before the weapon was fired. Spain's largest hotel chain pulling thirty-four properties out of Cuba in a single week because sanctions made it impossible to operate. Crypto exchanges having their cloud servers seized.

China running purges through six separate institutional domains  the energy sector, the securities regulator, the defense establishment, the Politburo itself, a transnational laundering conglomerate, and finally the national banking regulator. Saudi Arabia arresting two hundred and ninety government officials in two months. India raiding money laundering operations across multiple states. Russia purging its own oligarchs.

And in the spring of 2023 five financial institutions failed in eight weeks. Silvergate. Silicon Valley Bank. Signature. Credit Suisse. First Republic. Every one of them a bridge between the old rails and the new ones. Some paid fines and rebuilt their compliance function and survived. Some didn't survive. That is not a banking crisis. That is a sorting mechanism.

Every action follows the same construction schedule. Build the legal tool. Staff the institution. Fire the weapon. In that order. Every time.

EXHIBIT E The system was designed to survive its own disruption.

The United States maintains an active, continuously funded, heavily classified continuity of government architecture. Raven Rock Mountain Complex is a strategic battle-command platform their words, not mine undergoing forty-two million dollars in classified modernization right now. The FY2027 budget request for Raven Rock continuity equipment is explicitly classified.

The Emergency Federal Register maintained at a continuity facility in West Virginia ensures the government can continue publishing legally effective orders even if Washington is destroyed.

Presidential Emergency Action Documents pre-drafted classified executive orders sitting ready to sign have existed since the Cold War. As of 2017, there were reportedly fifty-six in effect. None has ever been declassified.

And on June 23, 2026 eleven weeks ago the White House published the America-First Resilience Strategy. It calls for distributed command and control across regions of the United States, secure networked communications, and continuity of the economy during disruption by preserving payments, liquidity, and trusted information flows.

Distributed command. Financial continuity. Payments. Liquidity. On the same page. From the White House.

EXHIBIT F The receipts arrive on a schedule.

Every OFAC sanctions notice in the Federal Register contains two dates. The date the action was issued and the date it was published. They are never the same. The action always comes first. The publication comes days or weeks later.

This is printed on every notice. In plain English. The government is telling you  on its own letterhead that the enforcement happened before you read about it.

The banks were already notified. The assets were already frozen. The target was already cut off. By the time the Federal Register publishes the notice, the operation is complete. The publication is the government telling the public what it already did.

Everything you read in the news is the last chapter of a story that started years ago.

EXHIBIT G  Now here's what cuts against me. 

I told you I'd show you this part.

In the last several weeks, four things happened that my framework did not predict and cannot easily absorb.

One. The beneficial ownership reporting requirement the rule that was going to force every American shell company to disclose who actually owns it was permanently eliminated for domestic companies. That was the single most important transparency rail in the entire architecture. It's gone. Foreign-owned entities still have to report. American ones don't.

Two. Enforcement of Russian sanctions evasion went quiet for seventeen months, then resumed. Seventeen months.

Three. Ahead of a summit in Alaska, sanctions were suspended by emergency authority. Not lapsed. Suspended. Deliberately.

Four. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's protective injunction was vacated. The agency that supervises the consumer end of the financial system is being dismantled.

All four of those happened while the same Treasury Department levied a record anti-money-laundering penalty against UBS, designated Iranian exchanges, and the Justice Department stood up a five-hundred-prosecutor fraud division.

Same government. Same Treasury. Same Secretary. Same week.

There are two honest ways to read that, and I cannot falsify either one.

The first reading is that this is a sorting mechanism operating by design. Enforcement expands against the network while supervision of ordinary business contracts. Front door opens, back door closes. Deliberate.

The second reading is simpler. It's one administration with contradictory policies, doing two incompatible things at once because different people are running different pieces.

I don't know which is true. Neither does anybody else who's honest about it. Both survive the evidence.

And Russia is the hardest case in the whole workbook. Russia purges its own oligarchs and receives sanctions accommodation in the same quarter. It is not cleanly activated. It is not cleanly accommodated. It is both, simultaneously, and I have watched the same waiver lapse and reissue twice now on a pattern I can document but cannot explain.

Nine years of tracking. Zero predictions falsified. And I want to be very direct with you about that number.

Zero falsifications is not a victory. It's a warning. A framework that never gets anything wrong is usually a framework that isn't specific enough to be wrong. That's why I write down, in advance, with hard dates, exactly what would prove me wrong. And that's why I'm reading you the four counter-signals instead of the four confirmations I could have picked instead.

THE QUESTION I'M ASKING YOU TO ANSWER

I'm not asking you to believe that a secret government is running the world from a bunker. I'm not asking you to believe in any conspiracy. I'm asking you to look at what the government itself has documented, published, and funded and ask yourself one question:

Does what you're watching on the news make more sense now?

Does the timing make more sense? Does the sequencing make more sense? Does a Chinese-funded INTERPOL operation arresting people in ninety-seven countries make more sense? Does nine sovereigns hitting the same cartel in eighteen months make more sense? Does the pattern build the tool, staff the institution, fire the weapon, every single time make more sense?

The machine was built after 9/11. The authorities that matter were stacked and never released. The intelligence was gathered for years while the networks operated. The map was drawn. The deals were made. The cooperators were turned. And then, starting in December 2017 and running every year since, the enforcement wave began.

Not in one country. In all of them.

Not against one target. Against the entire network class.

Not with one tool. With every legal authority accumulated over twenty-five years, stacked on top of each other, all active simultaneously, deployed through a system designed to survive anything.

Here's what I will not tell you.

I will not tell you it's finished. I will not tell you the good guys won. I will not tell you there's a date on the calendar when the curtain comes down and everything is made right in a single morning.

That's not the shape of this thing. This isn't a flood. It's an actuarial table. Slow. Distributed. Only legible in aggregate, and only in hindsight. Six hundred and thirty events don't feel like anything on any given Tuesday. Stacked on one timeline across nine years and forty jurisdictions, they look like something being built.

And it is still being built. Some floors are going up. One of them just came down.

What you are watching  right now, today, on your phone, in your newsfeed is not the investigation.

It's the receipts.

They spent twenty-five years building a machine that can follow every dollar on earth, freeze any account, cut off any bank, designate any target, seize any asset, survive any disruption, and coordinate across more than forty nations.

And now they're using it. 

Whether they use all of it, on everyone, is the part I'm still watching. So should you.

I am the guy on the couch, and you have been debriefed.

text:
Senior Researcher Dr. Sanjana Hattotuwa has raised questions over the continued visibility of betting-linked surrogate brands during Sri Lanka Cricket matches, despite regulatory action against unlicensed online gambling platforms in the country.

In an analysis of highlights from the second Test between Sri Lanka and India at the SSC, Hattotuwa said the 1xBAT logo received around 14 minutes of screen exposure across five daily highlights packages published by Sri Lanka Cricket.

The five videos had collectively recorded more than 629,000 views at the time of his analysis. Combined with highlights from the first Test in Galle, Hattotuwa estimated that 1xBAT received around 25 minutes of exposure across 10 videos viewed around two million times.

He said 1xBAT branding appeared through an advertising mat behind the wicket, boundary advertising and sight-screen placements during the SSC Test. Sri Lanka Cricket’s website confirms that official highlights from the Test were published on its channels.

Hattotuwa also highlighted the presence of Parimatch Sports and batbricks7 during the second Test, describing them as surrogate brands linked to offshore betting operations.

The researcher questioned how such advertising could continue while Sri Lankan authorities were taking action against unlicensed online gambling websites.

The Telecommunications Regulatory Commission of Sri Lanka had earlier moved to block access to several gambling websites, including https://t.co/hbVX8m2cGa. Hattotuwa argues that 1xBAT functions as a surrogate brand for 1xBet, an association that has previously been acknowledged by a former Sri Lanka Cricket secretary.

The Gambling Regulatory Authority Act No. 17 of 2025 includes provisions governing the operation and promotion of unlicensed online gambling.

Sri Lanka Cricket, however, has previously said it “does not permit betting advertising at SLC matches within the territory of Sri Lanka.”

text:
Wow!

"A Google data center is going up near West Memphis, Arkansas, and residents keep being told someone else is covering the cost for power. 

Jessica Kivell, a nurse, got curious, so she asked the state for paperwork.

The state sent Kivell the documents. She handed them to Sydney Sasser—a reporter at the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette—who published them on August 31. The paper reported on Google covering $526 million for a $1.6 billion solar plant that was built to feed the data center.

It also reported that power company Entergy was charging its customers $5.77 more per month since June that went to three new power projects—one of them the solar plant intended for the data center. 

Entergy wants a retraction. They claim the math is wrong. Entergy filed a lawsuit the next day, asking the judge to rule before Kivell or the newspapers could speak about it. 

They also demanded the article be taken down from the website, and asked the court to make all five defendants name anyone they shared the documents with. 

Their brief never mentioned the First Amendment.

But presiding Judge Lee Rudofsky did, calling it prior restraint and saying the matter was one of significant public concern. 

Kivell sat through the hearing in her work scrubs. Rudofsky refused to order the story taken down or to issue a gag order. A day later Entergy abandoned its bid for an injunction.

One person, one records request, and that story is still up."

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

Free ebook, free cleaning brush, free travel case — all listed as "$0.00" line items in the cart. They cost the brand almost nothing to include, but visually they make the 3x option look like it comes with a whole bonus package the 1x buyer doesn't get.

2. The most expensive tier is the pre-selected default

Notice the 3x option has the filled radio button, not the cheapest 1x. Most shoppers never touch the default — so the "decision" to spend 2x more was actually made for them before they scrolled to the checkout button.

3. Escalating savings % reframes spending more as saving more

29% → 44% → 53% off as quantity goes up. The math itself argues for the bigger order. By the time a buyer reaches the 3x tier, walking away feels like leaving money on the table instead of spending more of it.

4. Urgency closes the deal before comparison shopping happens

"Items in your cart are in high demand," a live countdown reserving the order — this isn't decoration, it's designed to convert the hesitation window before a 45+ buyer opens a new tab to price-check.

5. Why this determines who wins the ad auction, not just the sale

Anyone else just using a tasks folders as a ticket system? 

docs/tasks/
├── task-352-rate-limiter-rewrite/
├── task-353-zero-downtime-migrations/
├── task-354-postgres-sql-refactor/
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── plan.md
│   └── artifacts/
└── task-355-auth-token-rotation/

---
description: Condense scattered plans, progress, and research into one durable, sequentially-numbered task folder under docs/tasks/. Create a new task folder (handoff README + living plan checklist + research/), update an existing one, list open tasks, or close one out. Sweeps loose scratch files into the folder so any agent can pick the task up cold. Public, repo-agnostic version of /task.
argument-hint: "[description] | list | <task-ref> | update <task-ref> | done|block|pause|abandon <task-ref>"
---
# /task — Condense plans, progress & research into a handoff folder
> Generic, shareable version of the task-folder workflow. Drop it into your
> own repo as `.claude/commands/task.md` and adjust the paths and test
> commands to taste.
When a lot is in flight, planning, progress, decisions, and research end up
scattered across chat and loose files. This command turns all of that into
**one clean task folder** under `docs/tasks/` that a different agent can pick

up cold — whether you invoke it **at the start** of a task (mostly

scaffolding) or **halfway through** (gather + condense what already exists).
## Folder layout
Each task is a subfolder `NNNN-YYYY-MM-DD-three-word-slug/` holding:

```
README.md              ← handoff / orientation: goal, why, current state, key files, decisions, links, log
plan.md                ← the LIVING plan + progress checklist — the source of truth for "what's next"
research/              ← research docs, notes, transcripts, pasted dumps, query results, review verdicts
research/MANIFEST.md   ← one row per retained artifact: what it is, when, what produced it

prototypes/            ← throwaway code kept for reference: spike scripts, mockups, probe harnesses

artifacts/             ← binary/exported evidence: screenshots, CSV/JSON exports, benchmark output

```
`README.md` is what a fresh agent reads first; `plan.md` is what they work
from and tick off as they go. Create `prototypes/` and `artifacts/` only when
the task actually has such files — an empty scaffold folder is noise.
## Modes
Pick the mode from the argument:
- **(default / a description)** → **create** a new task and condense the current
conversation into it. e.g. `/task` or `/task wire the ad engine into the backend`.

- `list` → list open tasks. Scan the task folders directly (grep `**Status:**`
across `docs/tasks/*/README.md`), sort by **Updated** newest first, and call
out the **stale** ones (still `active`, not updated in ~14 days) as their own

group — those are usually finished-but-never-closed, not live work. With

many folders, delegate the scan to a background agent (see below).

- `<task-ref>` or `update <task-ref>` → **update** an existing task: tick items
in `plan.md` with dates + evidence, refresh **Current state** in the README,
append dated **Log** entries for every beat since the last update, **sweep
new scratch/prototype/artifact files into the folder and record them in
`research/MANIFEST.md`**, and bump **Updated**.
- `done <task-ref>` / `block <task-ref>` / `pause <task-ref>` /
`abandon <task-ref>` → set **Status** (`done` / `blocked` / `paused` /
`abandoned`), append a Log line explaining why, and bump **Updated**. For
`done` on a substantial programming effort, run the **Closeout checklist**
first.
If the mode is ambiguous, ask the user one short question rather than guessing.
### Status is a five-value enum — write it exactly
**Status** is one of exactly `active` · `blocked` · `paused` · `done` ·
`abandoned` — lowercase, bare, nothing else on the line. Variants like `✅`,
`DONE`, `shipped`, or `**LIVE**` make `list` mode's grep worthless and hide
which work is genuinely open. Put nuance in **Current state**, never in the
Status value.

**Close what is finished.** Whenever you touch a task and the work is in fact

finished, parked, or dead, flip Status in the same pass rather than leaving it

`active` forever. If you notice a *neighbouring* stale task while working, say
so and offer to close it — don't silently edit someone else's task.
### Resolve a task reference safely
Before any update, close, move, stage, or commit, resolve `<task-ref>` against
the immediate child folders of `docs/tasks/`:

- An exact full folder name resolves directly.
- A bare `NNNN` is accepted only when exactly one folder matches that prefix.
- If more than one folder matches, list the candidates and require the full
folder name from the user. Never infer the intended task from dates, titles,

or the current conversation.

- Bind the result once as the resolved full folder name and use only that path
for every subsequent read or mutation. Never use a `NNNN-*` pathspec for

edits, moves, staging, or commits — it can select another task or another
agent's work.
## Keep the artifacts: scratch, prototypes & the manifest
Scratch directories such as `temp/` are typically gitignored. Anything left
there is invisible to git, invisible to the next agent, and gone the moment
someone cleans up. This is the single biggest research leak in practice:
screenshots, probe scripts, and query dumps that informed real decisions end
up looking as if the work never happened.
**The rule: if it informed a decision, it belongs in the task folder.** Scratch

may *start* in `temp/`, but it gets swept into the task folder at every

`/task update`, at every milestone commit, and **mandatorily** at closeout.
Retain generously — a probe script, a rejected mockup, a raw query dump, a
review verdict, the screenshot that proved the bug are all cheap to keep and
expensive to re-derive.
**Name scratch by task from the start.** Create scratch as

`temp/<NNNN>-<slug>/` the moment a task number exists, so ownership is legible
to every session sharing the tree and the closing sweep is a single directory
move. Before a number exists, `temp/<slug>/` is fine — rename it once numbered.
**Where each kind of file lands:**
| Kind | Destination |
|---|---|

| Notes, analyses, transcripts, pasted dumps, query results, review verdicts | `research/` |
| Spike scripts, probe harnesses, HTML mockups, throwaway prototypes | `prototypes/` |
| Screenshots, CSV/JSON exports, benchmark output, logs kept as evidence | `artifacts/` |
| Something the task's own docs link to directly | task root |

**Maintain `research/MANIFEST.md`.** Every retained file gets one row, added
when it lands — not reconstructed at closeout. A file with no row is a file
nobody can interpret in three weeks:
```markdown
# Artifact manifest — NNNN-slug
| File | Date | What it is | Provenance / how to regenerate | Keep? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `research/exp1-baseline.md` | 2026-08-07 | Per-target wall times, serial run | `make test`, host idle | permanent |
| `artifacts/rotation-wedge.png` | 2026-08-07 | Screenshot proving the wedge at 14:02 | status dashboard, session id redacted | permanent |
| `prototypes/probe_supplier.py` | 2026-08-07 | One-off raw-API probe | needs `SUPPLIER_API_KEY`; superseded by the real client | reference only |
```
`Provenance` is the load-bearing column: the exact command, query, URL, or
script that produced the file, so a later agent can re-run it instead of

trusting a stale number.
**Size discipline.** Task folders are committed — keep them light:
- Nothing over ~5 MB, and no bulk binaries. Downsample screenshots; keep a

representative slice of a huge log plus the command that regenerates it.
- For anything genuinely large, keep the **summary + provenance row** in the
manifest and leave the blob in `temp/`, saying so explicitly in the row.
- Don't move in generated junk (`node_modules`, build output, coverage dirs,
`.venv`), shared or still-live code, or another task's files.
**Never `git add` a path under `temp/`.** Move the file into the task folder
first (`git mv` for tracked files, a plain move for untracked ones), then
stage the new path. Fix the obvious internal links in the task's own docs
after moving, and note anything you couldn't safely fix.
## Running log discipline
The **Log** in `README.md` is the task's narrative, and it is the most
neglected part of the workflow. A task whose only log line is "created" cannot
be handed off; the reader gets the destination without the route.
**Log at every beat, not once per `/task` invocation.** Append a line when:
- the task is created, and whenever its scope changes;
- a phase or meaningful chunk of implementation lands (with the commit);
- a verification runs — record the **actual number or result**, pass or fail;
- a decision is made — what was decided, why, and who decided it;
- **a dead end is hit** — what you tried, why it didn't work. Dead ends are the
highest-value entries in the whole folder and the ones most often deleted
instead of recorded. A later agent who doesn't know a path was already
walked will walk it again;
- an assumption is disproven, a surprise surfaces, or something is handed off;
- closeout.
**Format** — one line per beat, dated, evidence-bearing, newest last:
```markdown
- 2026-08-07 14:20 — `--jobs N` scheduler landed (a1b2c3d); 14/14 runner
tests green ×5. Serial default untouched.

- 2026-08-07 16:05 — DEAD END: tried lane-locking the SQL tests; unnecessary —
the conftest already creates a unique per-session DB. Reverted, see
`research/exp1-lane-analysis.md`.

```

Add a clock time when several entries share a day. Cite the artifact: commit
sha, `https://t.co/KLZaJsNzuI`, test result, measured value, or a `research/` path.
Never rewrite history — append a correcting line instead of editing an old
one. **Write the log as you go, not from memory at closeout** — a
reconstructed log silently drops the dead ends and surprises, which is exactly
the material worth keeping.

## Delegate breadth to background agents
Anything that is *reading widely* rather than *deciding* should go to a
background agent so the main turn keeps moving. Launch independent ones in a
single message so they run concurrently, then fold their output into the task

folder.

| Job | When |
|---|---|
| Prior-art sweep — has this been tackled before? which task folders, code, and docs touch it? | Before scaffolding a new task |

| `list` mode — scan the folders for Status/Updated/next-action | `list` |

| Scratch sweep — inventory `temp/` and the session's files; propose the move plan + draft manifest rows | Create, every update, closeout |
| Research digest — summarize a big log pull or benchmark run into a `research/` note | Whenever raw output exceeds a screen |
| Docs-drift and test-surface scans — which docs the diff invalidated, which suites cover the touched code | Closeout |
Rules:
- **Launch early, then keep working.** Fire the sweeps at the top of the turn
and do the writing while they run.
- **Read-only for search.** Reserve write-capable agents for the scratch sweep,
and even then have them *propose* the move plan for you to execute.
- **Exactly one writer per task file.** Other sessions may commit to the same
tree concurrently; two agents editing `plan.md` corrupts the handoff. You own

the task docs — agents return material, you write it.

- **Everything an agent produces gets a manifest row**, with the agent's
charter as its provenance.
- **Agents report, they don't conclude.** Treat their findings as claims to
verify against the code. Mark anything unverified as **assumed** in
**Current state**.
- Skip the fan-out for a small or obvious task; a two-file bugfix doesn't need
a research fleet.

## Commit at big points (auto-commit — don't ask)
Strategic local commits are **part of this command**. When you hit a commit
point, make the commit without asking — local commits are cheap and
reversible; the gated action is `git push`, never the commit. More small
checkpoints beat one giant end-of-session commit.
**Always commit:**

- right after the task folder is first **scaffolded**;

- after every **`update`** that folds in real progress;
- any time a **major part of the work completes** mid-task, even without an
explicit `/task` invocation;
- **mandatorily on `done` / `block` / `pause`** — never leave a closed-out or
parked task uncommitted.
Rules:
- **Write a descriptive commit message** naming the actual milestone, led by
the task number and slug: `task(0089): scaffold cloud-shield handoff + plan`,
`task(0089): phase 1 denylist research complete` — not `update task` or `wip`.
- **Commit locally only — never `git push`.** A push may trigger CI or a
deploy; let the user decide when to push.
- **Stage explicitly — never `git add -A` / `git add .` / `git commit -a`.**
Other agents may have in-flight work in the same tree. Name the paths:
`git add -- docs/tasks/<resolved-task-folder>/` plus any closely-related
files this effort produced.
## Adversarial review gates (larger tasks)
Bigger efforts — a new feature, multi-file change, subsystem rewrite, or any
money / auth / security / external-I/O surface — get **two independent review

passes** from a reviewer that did not write the work (a second model, a

separate subagent, or a review tool): one against the *plan* before the work
is built, one against the *final diff* before the task closes. Skip both for
small or doc-only tasks.
1. **Plan review (before/early in the build).** Once `plan.md` and `README.md`
exist, hand them to the reviewer read-only and ask it to challenge the
approach, sequencing, risks, and missing steps. Save the response under
`research/YYYY-MM-DD-plan-review.md`, fold the material points back into
`plan.md`, and note in the Log that the plan was reviewed — **before**
committing to the implementation, while feedback is still cheap.
2. **Adversarial diff review (at closeout).** Run an adversarial pass over the
finished diff that challenges design choices, assumptions, and failure
modes under real conditions — not just surface defects. Save the verdict
under `research/YYYY-MM-DD-adversarial-review.md`, address or consciously
accept each finding (record the disposition in the Log), and only then flip

Status to `done`.

## Create a task (default)
0. **Fire the background sweeps first** (skip for a small/obvious task): a
prior-art agent and a scratch-inventory agent, launched in one message.
Continue with the steps below while they work.

1. **Figure out the task.** Use the user's argument plus the conversation. If

the scope genuinely isn't clear, ask one concise question — but prefer
inferring from context. Decide a **3-word kebab slug** (e.g.
`ad-engine-wireup`, `sql-conn-budget`).
2. **Compute the folder name** `NNNN-YYYY-MM-DD-slug`. Number collisions are
the classic parallel-session bug: a stale checkout misses numbers another
session already pushed, and a sibling worktree may hold a number that isn't

on the remote yet. So take the max across local `docs/tasks/`, the remote

default branch, and any local `task/NNNN*` branches or worktrees:
```bash
d="docs/tasks"
git fetch origin main --quiet
local_n=$(ls "$d" 2>/dev/null | grep -Eo '^[0-9]{4}' | sort -n | tail -1)
remote_n=$(git ls-tree -d --name-only origin/main:docs/tasks 2>/dev/null \
| grep -Eo '^[0-9]{4}' | sort -n | tail -1)
n=$(printf '%s\n%s\n' "${local_n:-0}" "${remote_n:-0}" | sort -n | tail -1)
printf '%04d-%s-%s\n' "$((10#${n:-0}+1))" "$(date +%F)" "your-three-word-slug"

```

Re-check the candidate immediately before creating it. If a duplicate still
surfaces, renumber to the next free slot **before pushing**; if two folders
document the same effort, merge them rather than keeping both.
3. **Create the folder** `docs/tasks/NNNN-YYYY-MM-DD-slug/`.
4. **Gather & move loose files into the folder**, then **write
`research/MANIFEST.md`.** Find candidates (scratch dirs from this session,

loose plans or research docs, exported query results, screenshots,
benchmark output, one-off scripts, review verdicts); propose what lands
where; move it (`git mv` for tracked files, plain move for untracked);
rename the surviving scratch dir to `temp/<NNNN>-<slug>/`; write a manifest
row for every file moved in; fix obvious references. At the start of a task
there may be nothing to move — create the manifest with its header anyway.

5. **Write `plan.md`** — the living plan + progress checklist (template below).
Mid-task, reflect reality: mark already-done steps `[x]` **with the date and
evidence**, and put the next concrete action first.
- **Granularity:** each item is one sitting's work with an observable end
state. "Wire preflight gate" is a phase; "add `locatorFallback()` + unit
test for the re-chunked webview" is an item. If you cannot say what would

prove an item done, split it until you can.

- Give each phase an explicit **Exit criteria** line, decided *before* the
work.
- For a large task, run the **plan review** now and fold its points in

before building.
6. **Write `README.md`** — the handoff doc (template below). Be a fresh
agent's best friend: state **Goal** and **Why** so the task stands alone;
separate **verified** from **assumed** facts in **Current state**; list

**key files** with one line each on why they matter; record **decisions
already made** (with the why) and **constraints / things NOT to do**; keep
the detailed checklist in `plan.md` and just link to it.
7. **Don't maintain a shared per-task index table** in `docs/tasks/README.md`.
With many sessions working in parallel, one table everyone appends to is a
constant merge-conflict source. Discoverability comes from the folder name
(which sorts chronologically) and each task's own README header; `list`
mode scans the folders directly.
8. **Commit the scaffold** locally, e.g.
`task(NNNN): scaffold <slug> handoff + plan`. Don't ask; don't push.
9. **Report** the new task path, what you moved in, and a one-line summary of
what you captured. Offer to keep going on the task itself.
## `README.md` template (handoff / orientation)
```markdown
# <Task Title>
- **Task:** NNNN-YYYY-MM-DD-three-word-slug
- **Status:** active   <!-- active · blocked · paused · done · abandoned -->
- **Created:** YYYY-MM-DD
- **Updated:** YYYY-MM-DD
- **Owner:** @handle / agent
## Goal
One or two sentences: what "done" looks like.
## Why / context
Background a fresh agent needs — what triggered this, why it matters.
## Current state
What's true right now. Mark facts as **verified** vs **assumed**. What's done,
what's in flight, what's blocked.

## Plan

See [plan.md](plan.md) for the working checklist. Next up: <one line>.
## Key files & locations
- `path/to/file` — what it does / why it matters
- `research/<note>.md` — what's in it
- See [research/MANIFEST.md](research/MANIFEST.md) for every retained
artifact and how it was produced.
## Decisions & constraints
- Locked decisions (with the why), gotchas, things NOT to do.

## Dead ends
- What was tried and didn't work, and why — so nobody walks it twice.
## Open questions / risks
- ...
## Links
- Related tasks: NNNN-...
- PRs / commits / docs: ...
## Log
- YYYY-MM-DD — created; condensed from <where>; moved in <files>.
```
## `plan.md` template (living plan + progress checklist)

```markdown
# Plan — <Task Title>
> Working checklist. Tick items as they land; keep the next concrete action at
> the top of the current phase. Updated alongside the README.
>
> Every `- [x]` carries a **date** and the **evidence** that closed it — a

> commit sha, `https://t.co/KLZaJsNzuI`, a test result, or a measured number. An
> undated, unevidenced tick is a claim, not a record.
## Phase 1 — <name>
**Exit criteria:** <what must be observably true for this phase to be done>
- [ ] Next concrete action (first) — one sitting, observable end state

- [ ] ...
## Phase 2 — <name>

**Exit criteria:** <...>
- [ ] ...

## Done

- [x] 2026-08-07 — <what landed> (commit `a1b2c3d`; 14/14 runner tests green)
- [x] 2026-08-07 — <what landed> (measured 616s → 312s, see

`research/exp1-results.md`)
## Dead ends / rejected
- 2026-08-07 — tried <X>; didn't work because <Y>. Don't retry without <Z>.
## Notes
- Running progress notes, blockers hit, things tried.

```
## Closeout checklist (big programming efforts)

When a task was a substantial programming effort, don't close it the moment
the code first works. Before `done`, walk this short closeout so the next

agent inherits a clean, documented, tested surface:
0. **Final scratch sweep** — walk `temp/<NNNN>-*/` and the session's working
files one last time and move everything the task depended on into

`research/` / `prototypes/` / `artifacts/`, with a manifest row each. This
is the step most often skipped and the one that destroys the most research

— do it first, so the manifest is available to cite.
1. **READMEs** — update the README for every subsystem the effort touched, and
the root README if the repo map or data flow shifted. Add a "things that
have bitten us" entry for any new gotcha.
2. **Documentation** — refresh the canonical docs the change affects

(architecture notes, runbooks, contracts, test matrix) and fix now-stale
links or examples.

3. **Light audit** — a quick scoped pass over the diff: remove dead code,
tighten obvious rough edges, confirm nothing half-finished is left behind.

A tidy-up, not a rewrite.
4. **Tests** — exercise the new behavior with real tests and run the relevant

suite. Record pass/fail honestly in the Log; if something is red, say so
rather than closing over it.
5. **Adversarial diff review** — run the review-gate pass above, save the

verdict under `research/`, and address or consciously accept each finding.
Don't flip Status to `done` with unresolved findings hanging.
6. **Log it** — append a closeout entry naming what you updated, audited,

tested, and how the review was dispositioned. Then reread the whole **Log**

as a stranger would: if it doesn't tell the story of how this task went —
including the dead ends — fill the gaps now.

7. **Closing commit** — commit the closeout locally, e.g.
`task(NNNN): close out <slug> — <one-line outcome>`. A task is not `done`
until this commit exists; never push.
Skip this for small/non-code tasks — but **step 0 and the Log reread in step 6
are not optional at any size**: even a one-hour investigation should leave its
evidence and its narrative behind.

### Wrap-up status table
End the turn (and the closeout) with a compact status table. Use ✅ done /

good, ⚠️ partial or needs attention, ❌ not done / failing, and keep **Notes**
to one short line. Only mark ✅ for things you actually verified.

```markdown
| Check          | Status | Notes                                  |

| -------------- | :----: | -------------------------------------- |

| Scratch swept  |   ✅   | 7 files → research/ + artifacts/, manifest written |
| READMEs        |   ✅   | backend + client readmes refreshed     |
| Documentation  |   ⚠️   | architecture note updated; runbook TODO |
| Light audit    |   ✅   | clean, 1 dead fn removed               |

| Tests          |   ❌   | backend suite: 2 failing (auth)        |
| Review         |   ⚠️   | plan ✅; adversarial diff pass pending |

| Log complete   |   ✅   | 9 entries incl. 2 dead ends            |
| Task status    |   ⚠️   | active — tests must go green to close  |
```

Adapt the rows to the task; for small/non-code tasks just show **Status**,

**Next up**, **Blockers**. A red ❌ or amber ⚠️ means the task is **not**
ready for `done` — say so plainly.
## Notes

- **Auto-commit at milestones is expected**; **never deploy or `git push`**
as part of this command.
- **Keep `Updated`, the `plan.md` checklist, and the `Log` honest.** A stale
handoff misleads the next agent — that's worse than no doc.
- **`docs/tasks/` vs `temp/`:** scratch *starts* in `temp/<NNNN>-<slug>/`;
everything that informed a decision gets **moved into the task folder** with
a manifest row. The default outcome for anything left in `temp/` is
deletion, not archival.
- **When in doubt, keep it.** A retained prototype or raw dump costs a few KB;
re-deriving it costs a session. The failure mode is always under-retention,
never over-retention.
